::: callout-note
## What this is, and why it is not the note that was commissioned

Strand C was scoped as an **investigation**: three open questions that go beyond
what the contract builds, answered in a 5–10 page note recommending which
directions are worth pursuing, with rough effort estimates.

It has turned out differently, and better. **All three directions were partly
built during the contract** — not as a plan, but because each turned out to be
on the path to something the pilot needed. So this reports **what happened when
we tried them**, rather than what we expect might happen.

That includes one clear **negative result** (§C2), which is the most useful thing
in the note, and one finding that a decision made for privacy reasons has
**capped** what a whole research direction can measure (§C3).
:::

## The three questions

From the project's Strand C definition:

- **C1 — Beyond LLMs.** Are there model classes better than, or supplementary to,
  LLMs for some of the project's tasks? What is available, what is GDPR-tractable,
  what would it cost to host, and where does each class shine or fail for
  upper-secondary physics?
- **C2 — Beyond chat.** Chat is the default interface but probably not the right
  one for every physics task. Voice, branching, concept-map interfaces all have a
  case. One concrete option to investigate: a Plaud-like setup that records a
  student group's discussion, transcribes it, and has AI analyse it.
- **C3 — Student models.** Can an AI maintain and update a model of a student's
  understanding over a topic — as a network of concepts and relations — and
  compare it to a reference model of the same topic?

## C1 — Beyond LLMs

### What we did

We built a benchmark harness (`stx-bench`) that measures model performance
against **Danish stx Fysik A written-exam problems**, calibrated against official
answer keys first and then used for tier descent — working down a model panel to
find where capability falls away, overall and per physics topic. Text and figure
tasks were measured separately.

The detailed results are in the companion note *"Which AI model is good enough
for which task"* (2026-08-27).

::: callout-warning
### A constraint on this section

The exam corpus is drawn from **Prøvebanken**, and legal approval for its use is
**pending with the Ministry of Education**. We hold model-performance results
against that corpus and have decided **not to publish them** until approval is
granted. This note therefore states conclusions at a level the approval does not
gate, and the underlying numbers stay internal for now.
:::

### What we found

**1. For this task class, self-hosting is already viable.** The July 2026
snapshot puts several open-weight tiers over the practical floor on both text and
figures. The migration trigger the project defined — an eval gate plus a hosting
gate — is **met on the eval side** for stx physics.

**2. A self-hosted tier needs two models, not one.** This is the finding with the
most consequence for anyone planning a model catalogue. Text competence and
figure competence do not arrive together: a model that solves the written problem
cannot necessarily read the graph attached to it. **Any serious self-host plan
needs a text model *and* a vision-language model**, and budgeting for one is the
common mistake.

**3. Published benchmarks mis-rank the cheap candidates.** Ranking by public
leaderboard would have chosen differently from ranking by measured performance on
this task. For a subject-specific decision, the subject-specific measurement is
not optional.

### Does this answer "beyond LLMs"?

**Partly, and the honest answer includes what we did not do.**

- **Vision-language models** were the obvious candidate and are now *inside* the
  system rather than beside it — not an alternative to the LLM but a **required
  second tier**. That is the answer to the question as asked.
- **Embodied and world-model classes** were named in the original scoping and
  **were not investigated**. Saying so plainly is better than a paragraph of
  speculation. Nothing in the pilot created a reason to, and nothing we saw
  suggests they are near-term for written physics tasks.

### Recommendation for C1

**Pursue as maintenance, not as a workstream.** The instrument exists; the
valuable thing is now **re-running it** as models release — quarterly is the
natural cadence, and it is the input to both the model catalogue and the
self-hosting decision.

**Effort:** ~0.5–1 day per re-run once the runbook exists (that runbook is
outstanding and is on the handover list). **Do not** open an embodied/world-model
investigation this year.

## C2 — Beyond chat

This is the section with a real result, and it is a negative one.

### The Plaud-like prototype was built, and it failed at classroom scale

The concrete option named in the scoping — record a group's discussion,
transcribe, analyse — was built and run for the first time at genuine classroom
scale on **16 June 2026**.

**It did not work.** The capture pipeline was healthy, the service was up, the
data flowed, and the transcripts were **largely unusable**: roughly 40% of
segments empty or garbled.

### The diagnosis, which is the transferable part

The failure was **not in capture** — it was in **transcription**, and
specifically in **Danish–English code-switching**. Danish physics teaching mixes
English technical vocabulary freely; the speech service, configured for Danish,
returned empty or garbage on English-dominant audio.

Re-running the *same audio* through two configurations:

| Configuration | Usable output |
|---|---|
| Cloud STT v1 `latest_long`, Danish only *(what was in production)* | **360 characters** — gibberish; the demo failure reproduced |
| A general multimodal model prompted to transcribe verbatim, keeping each phrase in its own language | **8,251 characters** of clean Danish |

**A general-purpose multimodal model beat a purpose-built speech service by more
than twenty times on usable output**, on the same recording, for this bilingual
classroom case. The fix has since shipped.

### Two findings worth carrying

**1. For bilingual classroom audio, the general model beat the specialist
service.** That is directly relevant to C1's question about model classes, and it
is the opposite of the intuition that a purpose-built service wins on its own
task.

**2. The failure was silent, and that is the pattern.** Every dashboard was
green. The service reported success. The data arrived. Only the *content* was
worthless — and nobody would have known without opening a transcript and reading
it. This is the same failure class the project has met repeatedly, and the
lesson generalises past physics: **a pipeline that reports success is not
evidence that it produced anything usable.**

### "Beyond chat" turned out to be the default, not the experiment

The broader C2 question has been answered by building. The product is now mostly
**not** a chat window:

- an interactive **workbench** — data tables, plots, calculators, checklists,
  written answers, image and freehand submission — whose state the tutor can see;
- **simulations** as first-class objects the tutor reacts to;
- a **concept-map** interface (see C3);
- **voice** output, with configurable styles.

The teaching value did not come from a better chat interface. It came from the
tutor being able to **see what the students did** — the table they filled, the
simulation they ran — rather than only what they typed.

### Recommendation for C2

**The interface question is answered; treat it as settled.** The remaining C2
work is narrow and specific: the research-audio pipeline is **fixed but not yet
re-validated at classroom scale**. It should be re-run at the next real session
before anyone relies on it as research data.

**Effort:** ~0.5 day to validate at the next session. The Plaud-like *analysis*
layer on top of good transcripts is unstarted and is a reasonable Year-2 item
(~3–5 days), but it is worth nothing until transcript quality is confirmed in a
real room a second time.

## C3 — Student models

The most speculative of the three, the one the team was most excited about, and
the one where the finding is genuinely unexpected.

### The representation half works, and is running

A **concept map** is now a first-class part of an activity, shipped to the
development environment:

- a teacher authors a **prerequisite graph** of concepts for the activity, or has
  the authoring co-pilot propose one;
- students see their own progress across it;
- the tutor runs **in-conversation checkpoints** and records which concepts a
  group has demonstrated;
- the map **lights up** as understanding is evidenced, stored per group.

So the core C3 mechanic — *maintain a structured model of understanding, updated
from free-form dialogue, against a reference map for the topic* — **is not
speculative any more. It runs.** LLMs did change the arithmetic of building
these models, as the scoping hoped: the extraction is the cheap part.

### The blocker is calibration, and it is a research problem

The design work names it plainly: **the evaluation is the long pole**, not the
extraction.

The system can say a group has demonstrated understanding of a concept. **Nobody
has yet measured whether it is right.** Doing that means human raters scoring a
sample against the AI's judgement, an agreement measure, and a decision about
what agreement is good enough to show a teacher. Until then the map is a
*plausible* picture of understanding, and the distance between plausible and
validated is the entire research contribution.

### The finding nobody planned: privacy has capped the granularity

**A decision taken for data-protection reasons has bounded what C3 can measure,
and this deserves to be stated as a result rather than discovered later.**

AIPLA's foundational decision is that the **group, not the student, is the unit**:
students join anonymously by group code, and no personal identity is collected.
That is what makes the platform defensible in a school, and it is not in question.

But C3 asks about **a student's** understanding. What the system can actually
maintain is a **group's** understanding. For a pair or trio at one table those are
close; they are not the same, and the difference is exactly where the interesting
questions live — who in the group is carrying the reasoning, who is quiet, who
diverges from the reference model.

Reaching per-student granularity is **not a feature** — it is a revision of the
foundational anonymity decision, with consent and governance consequences. It is
scoped as an open question in its own right.

**So C3 has to be understood as a group-level instrument unless and until that
decision is deliberately revisited.** That is a real constraint on the research
value, and it is the honest headline of this section.

### Recommendation for C3

**Pursue, and invest the effort in calibration rather than in features.** This is
the direction with genuine novelty, and it is closer to working than expected —
which makes the temptation to add capability before validating the capability
that exists the main risk.

Concretely, in order:

1. **Calibrate the existing check-off.** Human raters, a sample, an agreement
   number, published alongside any teacher-facing use. *~2–3 days engineering plus
   researcher rating time.*
2. **Teacher coverage view** — what the class as a whole has and has not
   evidenced. *~1–1.5 days.* Only after (1).
3. **Decide the group-vs-student question explicitly**, as a governance question
   with the data-protection owners, not as a backlog item. *Discussion, not
   engineering.*
4. **Cross-group comparison** — how a class converges or diverges from the
   reference map — is the natural research instrument and should wait for (1).
   *Year-2.*

## Summary of recommendations

| Direction | Verdict | Next step | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| **C1 — beyond LLMs** | **Answered.** VLMs are a required second tier, not an alternative class. Embodied/world models: not now | Re-run the eval quarterly | ~0.5–1d per run |
| **C2 — beyond chat** | **Answered by building.** The value came from the tutor seeing student work, not from a better chat window | Re-validate research audio at the next real session | ~0.5d, then Year-2 for analysis |
| **C3 — student models** | **Pursue.** Representation works; validation does not exist yet | Calibrate the check-off against human raters | ~2–3d + rating time |

**If only one thing is done from this note, it should be the C3 calibration.** It
is the only item that converts something the project has already built into
something it can defend as a finding.

## Limitations

- **The C1 numbers are withheld** pending Prøvebanken approval; conclusions here
  are stated at a level that approval does not gate.
- **C2's negative result comes from one session** (16 June). The diagnosis was
  reproduced on the same audio under two configurations, which is strong for the
  *cause* and weak for the *prevalence*.
- **C3's mechanic is running in the development environment**, not in classrooms
  at scale. "It works" means "it does the thing", not "it does the thing well" —
  which is the calibration gap this note recommends closing.
- **Embodied and world-model classes were not investigated.** They remain open,
  not dismissed.
- Broader classroom trials are **pending a data-processing agreement**, currently
  targeted for late 2026, which bounds how much more evidence any of these three
  directions can accumulate this year.

## The single sentence

Two of the three directions were answered by building them — the useful model
class was a vision-language tier rather than a new paradigm, and the value beyond
chat came from the tutor seeing student work rather than from a better
conversation — while the third, modelling what students understand, now runs and
needs validating rather than extending.
